steps.body:
A complex number a + bi is a POINT (a, b) in the plane — so it has polar coordinates too (recall Ch1). Its distance from the origin is the **modulus** r = √(a² + b²); its angle is the **argument** θ. This gives the **polar (trig) form**:

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ).
A complex number already has a length and an angle.

widget.prompt: Plot 3 + 4i, then read its length off the display.
widget.successFeedback: |z| = 5, from 3² + 4² = 25 — Pythagoras, on the Argand plane. Polar form is nothing new: it is this same arrow, described by how long it is and which way it points instead of how far right and how far up.
widget.realFeedback: The real part is off — that is the distance right along the real axis.
widget.imagFeedback: The real part is right; the imaginary part is the height above the real axis.

cml.actionGoal: Move complex-number components and connect algebraic multiplication with geometric scale and rotation.

predict.prompt: 3 + 4i is plotted as the point (3, 4). Its modulus — its distance from the origin — is…
predict.reveal: 5. The modulus is Pythagoras applied to the real and imaginary parts, exactly as a vector's length is Pythagoras applied to its components. 3 + 4i and ⟨3, 4⟩ are the same arrow in different notation, and the modulus is where that stops being a metaphor.

steps.body: Match a to the real part.
explanationVariants: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) means a = r cos θ and b = r sin θ — exactly the polar→rectangular formulas (recall Ch1), now with i marking the vertical part.
The real part is r cos θ; the imaginary coefficient is r sin θ.

widget.prompt: In z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), the real part a equals:

commonBuilds.feedback: r sin θ is the IMAGINARY coefficient b (vertical). The real part is r cos θ.
Don't drop the modulus: a = r cos θ, scaled by the distance r.

widget.missFeedback: The real part is the horizontal projection x = r cos θ — modulus times cosine.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the same x = r cos θ from polar conversion; the real axis is horizontal.

steps.body: Going from rectangular to polar reuses Ch1's method: r = √(a² + b²), and θ = the angle whose tangent is b/a — **with the quadrant check** (recall the arctan trap). For z = 1 + i: r = √2 and θ = π/4, so z = √2(cos π/4 + i sin π/4).

explanationVariants: z = −1 + i is in Quadrant II: r = √2, and the reference angle π/4 becomes θ = 3π/4.
Both parts have size 1 but a < 0 < b, so the point sits in Q2 at 3π/4.

widget.prompt: The argument of z = −1 + i is:

options.label: 3π/4
options.feedback: Right — Q2 (real negative, imaginary positive): π − π/4 = 3π/4.

options.label: π/4
options.feedback: π/4 is Quadrant I. Here a = −1 < 0, so the point is in Q2: 3π/4.

options.label: −π/4
options.feedback: That's Q4. With a < 0 and b > 0 the point is in Q2: 3π/4.

explanationVariants: The 1-√3 leg ratio is the 30-60-90 signature: argument π/3, modulus 2.

widget.prompt: Write z = 1 + i√3 in polar form.

commonBuilds.feedback: tan θ = b/a = √3/1 = √3, which is π/3, not π/6 (that's tan = 1/√3).
r = √(1² + (√3)²) = √4 = 2, not 4 — don't skip the root.

widget.missFeedback: Modulus r = √(1 + 3) = 2; argument tan θ = √3 → π/3. Build 2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3).
widget.successFeedback: Right — r = √(1 + 3) = 2 and tan θ = √3 → θ = π/3 in Q1.

explanationVariants: z = −1 − i√3: r = 2; both parts negative → Q3. Reference angle π/3, so θ = π + π/3 = 4π/3. Enter 4π/3 as a decimal ≈ 4.19.
Q3 adds π to the reference angle: 4π/3 ≈ 4.1888.
hints: Reference angle π/3, plus π for Q3.

widget.prompt: The argument of z = −1 − i√3 (in [0, 2π)) is 4π/3. Enter it as a decimal to hundredths.

commonErrors.feedback: 1.05 ≈ π/3 is the reference angle only. In Q3 add π: 4π/3 ≈ 4.19.
2.09 ≈ 2π/3 is Q2. Both parts here are negative → Q3: 4π/3 ≈ 4.19.

takeaways: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) with r = √(a² + b²), θ from b/a plus a quadrant check.
a = r cos θ, b = r sin θ — the Ch1 conversion formulas.
Polar form makes multiplication and powers easy — next.
steps.teaser: Next: why polar form turns multiplication into a single rotation.

concept.body: Polar form: r = √(a²+b²); θ = angle of (a,b) with a quadrant check; then z = r(cos θ + i sin θ).

explanationVariants: Pure imaginary i sits distance 1 from the origin.

widget.prompt: What is the modulus of z = i?

commonErrors.feedback: i = 0 + 1i has imaginary part 1, so |z| = √(0 + 1) = 1, not 0.
Modulus is a DISTANCE, never negative: |i| = 1.
